title: Stars, Faith, and a Covenant Cut in the Dark
summary: God tells a childless Abram that he will have a son of his own and descendants as many as the stars, and Abram believes him. When Abram asks how he can know he will possess the land, God has him cut animals in half, foretells four centuries of slavery and a return, and then passes alone between the pieces as a smoking firepot and a flaming torch, binding himself by covenant.
story: In Genesis 12 God promised Abram land, a great nation, and blessing for every family on earth. Years have passed, and Abram has just rescued Lot from four invading kings (Genesis 14), yet he still has no child. The promise of a nation hangs on a son who doesn't exist. This chapter is where the promise becomes a covenant, a solemn and binding commitment, and where Abram's response is named for the first time as faith. It also looks far ahead, past Abram's death, through slavery in a foreign land, to the exodus and the return to Canaan.
historical: Those who read Genesis's chronology as history usually set Abram in the early second millennium BC, roughly 2000 to 1700 BC; other scholars doubt the patriarchal stories can be dated, or see them as traditions shaped much later. The childless man whose servant would inherit has been compared with tablets from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia (around the fifteenth and fourteenth centuries BC), where childless couples sometimes adopted an heir, with the arrangement changing if a natural son was later born. Mid-twentieth-century scholars leaned hard on such parallels; later work, notably by Thomas L. Thompson and John Van Seters in the 1970s, showed that many were overstated and that similar customs span a long period. The broad point stands: a household without a son needed a legal heir, and Abram has only Eliezer, a servant from Damascus.
cultural:
The ritual in verses 9 to 17 was a known way of making a binding agreement. Hebrew speaks of cutting a covenant, and here the phrase is literal. Jeremiah 34:18-20 describes Judah's leaders making a covenant by cutting a calf in two and walking between its parts. The meaning is a self-curse: may what happened to these animals happen to me if I break my word. An eighth-century BC Aramaic treaty from Sefire in Syria contains a similar curse.

What would have startled an ancient reader is who walks the path. Normally the party taking the oath passes between the pieces. Here Abram doesn't walk at all. He falls into a heavy sleep, and a smoking firepot and a flaming torch, signs of God's presence, pass through alone. God binds himself. The fire and smoke anticipate how God later appears to Israel, in the pillar of cloud and fire and in the smoke on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18).
literary: The chapter has two matching halves, each opening with God's self-introduction and Abram's question. In verses 1 to 6 God is Abram's shield and reward; Abram asks what God can give a childless man; God answers with the stars; Abram believes. In verses 7 to 21 God is the one who brought Abram from Ur; Abram asks, “how can I know that I will possess it?”; God answers with a covenant ritual. The first half turns on seeing the night sky, the second on darkness, deep sleep, and terror. Verse 6, a single sentence of the narrator's comment, sits at the hinge.

outline.t: A son and descendants like the stars; Abram believes
Abram asks for assurance and prepares the animals
In deep darkness, God foretells slavery and return
God passes between the pieces and makes a covenant

doctrines.note: Abram is old and his wife barren, yet “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (15:6). Faith here is not a feeling but reliance on the one who made the promise.
God alone passes between the pieces, taking the obligation on himself. The promise rests on God's commitment rather than Abram's performance, which becomes the pattern of grace throughout Scripture.
Righteousness is counted to Abram because he believes, before any law and before circumcision (Genesis 17). Paul builds his teaching on justification by faith directly on this verse.

words.note: Aman, to be firm or reliable; in the form used here, to believe or trust. It is the root behind the word amen. To believe is to lean one's weight on someone as trustworthy. Verse 6 is the verb's first appearance in the Bible.

Chashav, to think, reckon, or count, including in the sense of crediting something to an account. The same verb is used when a sacrifice is or isn't credited to the worshiper (Leviticus 7:18). God counts Abram's trust as righteousness.

Berit, covenant: a formal, binding bond between parties, sealed with oaths and signs. The Bible's story is carried by a series of covenants, with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, David, and the new covenant Jeremiah promised.

christ: Genesis 15:6 is among the Old Testament verses the New Testament quotes most. Paul uses it in Romans 4 and Galatians 3 to argue that God counts people righteous through faith, not works of the law, noting that Abram was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so that he is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike. James 2:23 cites it to insist that real faith shows itself in obedience. Hebrews 6:13-18 points to God binding himself by oath to Abraham as an anchor for Christian hope. Many Christians also see in God's walking alone between the pieces a picture of grace that takes the curse on itself, and connect it with the cross; that is a theological reading of the pattern, not a link the New Testament draws from this passage.

hard.q: Why must the land wait because “the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete”?
hard.a:
Verse 16 looks ahead to Israel's conquest of Canaan, which troubles many readers because of its violence. The verse itself frames that later event as judgment on long-standing wrongdoing, not ethnic favoritism, and it shows God waiting four centuries rather than acting at once. Leviticus 18:24-28 later warns Israel that the land will expel them too if they do the same things. Readers still differ on how to take the conquest accounts (some read their language of total destruction as ancient war rhetoric, others more literally), but this verse presents a God patient with nations outside his covenant who holds his own people to the same standard.

The numbers also puzzle readers: four hundred years in verse 13, the fourth generation in verse 16, and 430 years in Exodus 12:40. Many take four hundred as a round figure and read generation here as a full lifespan, since the Hebrew word can also mean an era.

questions: Abram believed God when nothing in his circumstances supported the promise. What makes trusting a promise hard when you can't see how it could come true?
God, not Abram, walks between the pieces. How does it change your view of God to see him bind himself to his promises rather than wait for us to earn them?
The chapter holds both a bright night of stars and a dark vision of slavery. Why might God tell Abram about the suffering ahead as well as the blessing?
